question: What is the MVC design pattern?
title: MVC Pattern Explained — Model, View, Controller
direct_answer: **MVC (Model-View-Controller)** is an architectural pattern that separates an application into three components: **Model** (data and business logic), **View** (presentation/UI), and **Controller** (handles HTTP requests, coordinates model and view). It promotes separation of concerns.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying MVC is a Spring-specific pattern — it's a general design pattern from the 1970s
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Spring MVC implements MVC with DispatcherServlet as the front controller

sections.title: MVC Components
sections.content:
**MVC** splits application responsibility into three layers:

- **Model**: Business logic and data — entities, services, repositories. Knows nothing about the UI.
- **View**: Presentation layer — Thymeleaf templates, JSP, or JSON for APIs. Knows nothing about business logic.
- **Controller**: Coordination layer — receives HTTP requests, calls the service/model, and returns a response (view or JSON).

The benefit: each layer can change independently. You can swap Thymeleaf for React without touching business logic.

sections.title: MVC in Spring Framework
sections.content:
- **Model**: `@Entity` classes, `@Service` beans, `@Repository` interfaces — pure business logic
- **View**: Thymeleaf templates (HTML), or JSON response (for REST APIs)
- **Controller**: `@Controller` (returns view name) or `@RestController` (returns data/JSON)
- **DispatcherServlet**: Spring's front controller — receives ALL requests and routes to correct controller
- **`@Controller`**: Traditional MVC — return string view name, resolved by ViewResolver
- **`@RestController`**: API-oriented — return data object, serialized to JSON by Jackson
- **`Model` object**: Map passed to view — controller puts data in Model, view reads it
- **Spring MVC flow**: Request → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → Controller → Service → DB → View/JSON

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: MVC stands for Model-View-Controller and it's an architectural pattern that separates an application into three layers. The Model is your business logic and data — entities, services, repositories. The View is the presentation — HTML templates or JSON responses. The Controller is the glue — it receives HTTP requests, calls the right service methods, and sends back a response. Spring MVC implements this pattern with DispatcherServlet as a front controller that receives every request and routes it to the appropriate controller method. For REST APIs you use @RestController which skips the view layer and returns JSON directly. The big benefit is separation of concerns — you can change your UI without touching business logic.

question: What is the difference between @Controller and @RestController?
title: @Controller vs @RestController in Spring MVC
direct_answer: **`@Controller`** returns a **view name** (resolved to HTML by ViewResolver — used in Thymeleaf MVC apps). **`@RestController`** = `@Controller + @ResponseBody` — returns data objects serialized to **JSON/XML** by Jackson, not a view. Use `@RestController` for REST APIs.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Controller for REST API and forgetting @ResponseBody — gets view resolution error
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain @ResponseBody and that @RestController is a composed annotation

sections.title: @Controller vs @RestController
Key Differences
sections.content:
- **`@Controller`**: Each method returns a view name string → passed to `ViewResolver` → resolves to HTML template
- **`@RestController`**: Returns data objects → `HttpMessageConverter` (Jackson) → JSON/XML response
- **`@RestController` = `@Controller + @ResponseBody`**: It's a composed annotation
- **`@ResponseBody`**: Can add this individually to methods in a @Controller to return JSON from specific methods
- **Mixed use**: `@Controller` with `@ResponseBody` on some methods = same as @RestController on those methods
- **Spring Boot + `@RestController`**: Jackson is auto-configured — returns JSON by default
- **Content-Type header**: @RestController sets `Content-Type: application/json` automatically

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RestController is just @Controller plus @ResponseBody — it's a shorthand composite annotation. The difference is in what happens to the return value. With @Controller, the return value is treated as a view name and gets passed to a ViewResolver to find the corresponding HTML template. With @RestController, the return value is the actual response body — Jackson serializes it to JSON and sends it back. For any REST API, you'd use @RestController. If you're building a traditional server-rendered web app with Thymeleaf, you'd use @Controller. The @ResponseBody annotation can also be added to individual methods inside a @Controller if you only want some methods to return JSON.

question: What is separation of concerns in MVC?
title: Separation of Concerns in MVC — Why It Matters
direct_answer: **Separation of concerns** in MVC means each layer has a single, well-defined responsibility: Controller handles HTTP, Service handles business logic, Repository handles data access, View handles presentation. No business logic in controllers or views — each layer can change independently.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why MVC layering matters beyond just knowing the names
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting business logic in controllers (fat controllers) — breaks separation of concerns
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe what goes in each layer with concrete Spring examples

sections.title: What Goes in Each Layer
sections.content:
**Clean Spring layering:**

- **Controller** (`@RestController`): Parse HTTP request, validate input, call service, return response. No SQL. No business rules.
- **Service** (`@Service`): Business logic, transactions, orchestration. Calls repositories. No HTTP awareness.
- **Repository** (`@Repository`): Data access only. JPA queries. No business logic.
- **Entity/DTO**: Data carriers — entities for DB, DTOs for HTTP layer.

sections.title: Separation of Concerns Benefits
sections.content:
- **Testability**: Service can be unit tested without HTTP or DB context
- **Maintainability**: Change UI framework without touching business logic
- **Reusability**: Service can be called from REST controller, messaging consumer, batch job
- **Single Responsibility Principle**: Each class has one reason to change

**Common violations to avoid:**
- **Fat controllers**: Business logic in @RestController methods
- **Anemic service**: Service just delegates to repository with no logic — service layer adds no value
- **Entity in response**: Returning JPA entities directly from API (exposes DB structure, breaks encapsulation)
- **SQL in controller**: Direct EntityManager or JDBC calls from controller

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Separation of concerns in MVC means each layer has one job and doesn't bleed into others. Controllers handle the HTTP stuff — parsing requests, calling the service, building the response. Services contain the actual business logic and are where transactions live. Repositories handle database access. This matters because if you put business logic in your controller, you can't reuse it from a scheduled job or message consumer — it's trapped in HTTP context. If you put SQL in your service, testing requires a running database. Clean separation means each layer is independently testable and swappable. The most common violation I've seen in fresher code is fat controllers that contain business logic directly — that's a design smell worth pointing out in an interview.

question: What is @RequestMapping in Spring MVC?
title: @RequestMapping in Spring MVC — URL Mapping and HTTP Methods
direct_answer: **`@RequestMapping`** maps HTTP requests to controller methods or classes. At the class level it sets the base URL path; at the method level it refines with sub-path and HTTP method. Shorthand annotations `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, etc., are composites of `@RequestMapping`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Spring MVC URL mapping knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not using shorthand annotations (@GetMapping, @PostMapping) — verbose @RequestMapping(method=GET) is dated style
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain composed annotations and show class-level + method-level combination

sections.title: @RequestMapping Usage
@RequestMapping and HTTP Method Annotations
sections.content:
- **`@RequestMapping("/path")`**: Works for all HTTP methods — use at class level for base path
- **`@GetMapping`** = `@RequestMapping(method=RequestMethod.GET)`
- **`@PostMapping`** = `@RequestMapping(method=RequestMethod.POST)`
- **`@PutMapping`** = full replace; `@PatchMapping` = partial update
- **`@DeleteMapping`** = HTTP DELETE
- **`produces`**: Restrict response content type: `@GetMapping(produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)`
- **`consumes`**: Restrict accepted request content type: `@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)`
- **Multiple paths**: `@RequestMapping({"/api/users", "/api/people"})` — map multiple URLs to same method

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @RequestMapping is the base annotation in Spring MVC for mapping HTTP requests to controller methods. You typically use it at the class level to define a base URL path — like /api/users — and then use the more specific shorthand annotations @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, and @PatchMapping on individual methods for the HTTP verb. These shorthand annotations are just composed versions of @RequestMapping with the method already filled in. You can also use produces and consumes on any of these to restrict which content types the endpoint accepts or returns.

question: What is the Model in Spring MVC?
title: Model in Spring MVC — Passing Data from Controller to View
direct_answer: In Spring MVC, the **`Model`** is a key-value map passed from a `@Controller` method to the view template. You add attributes with `model.addAttribute("key", value)` and access them in Thymeleaf/JSP templates with `${key}`. For REST APIs, the 'model' is essentially the Java object returned by the method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how data flows from controller to view in Spring MVC
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring MVC's Model object with the conceptual 'Model' layer (services/entities)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Differentiate between the 'M' in MVC (conceptual, means business logic layer) vs Spring's Model interface (a container for view data)

sections.title: Spring MVC Model
Model, ModelMap, ModelAndView
sections.content:
- **`Model`**: Interface — `addAttribute(String, Object)` — Spring injects it automatically
- **`ModelMap`**: Concrete implementation — same API, can be used as Model
- **`ModelAndView`**: Combines model data + view name in one return object
- **`@ModelAttribute`**: Method-level — adds attribute to model for all methods in controller; Parameter-level — binds form data
- **For REST APIs**: You don't use Model — you just return the Java object as method return value
- **`RedirectAttributes`**: Special model for redirect scenarios (preserves data through redirect)
- **Conceptual 'M' in MVC**: The domain/service/entity layer — not the same as Spring's Model interface

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: In Spring MVC, the Model is a map-like container that you use to pass data from your controller to the view template. In a @Controller method, you accept Model as a parameter — Spring injects it — and use addAttribute to put data in. The Thymeleaf or JSP template then accesses those values by their key names. It's important to distinguish this from the 'M' in MVC conceptually — when we say Model layer in architecture, we mean the business logic and entity layer. Spring's Model interface is specifically about the data passed to the view. For REST APIs using @RestController, you don't use Model at all — you just return the Java object directly and Jackson serializes it to JSON.

question: What is the difference between Spring MVC and Spring REST?
title: Spring MVC vs Spring REST — View-Based vs API-Based
direct_answer: **Spring MVC** (traditional) renders server-side HTML views using Thymeleaf/JSP. **Spring REST** returns data (JSON/XML) directly — no view templates. Both use the same DispatcherServlet infrastructure; the difference is the controller annotation (`@Controller` vs `@RestController`) and response type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Clarity on when to use MVC vs REST approach
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring REST is a completely different framework — it uses the same DispatcherServlet/MVC infrastructure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring REST is Spring MVC with @ResponseBody — same infrastructure, different output

sections.title: Spring MVC vs Spring REST
sections.content:
| Aspect | Spring MVC (View) | Spring REST |
|--------|-------------------|-------------|
| Controller | `@Controller` | `@RestController` |
| Response | HTML view (Thymeleaf) | JSON/XML data |
| Client | Browser | Any (mobile, JS, microservice) |
| View layer | Yes (templates) | No templates |
| Content-Type | `text/html` | `application/json` |
| Jackson | Not needed | Required |
| Session | Often used | Stateless (no session) |

sections.title: Same Infrastructure, Different Output
sections.content:
- Both use `DispatcherServlet` as front controller
- Both use `HandlerMapping` to find controller methods
- Both use `@RequestMapping` / `@GetMapping` etc.
- **Spring MVC**: Returns view name → `ViewResolver` finds template → Thymeleaf renders HTML
- **Spring REST**: Returns Java object → `HttpMessageConverter` (Jackson) → JSON in response body
- **Mixing**: One Spring Boot app can have both `@Controller` for pages and `@RestController` for API
- **Modern approach**: Most Spring Boot apps are REST-only, with React/Angular frontend consuming the API
- **spring-boot-starter-web**: Brings both MVC and REST capabilities

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring MVC and Spring REST use the exact same underlying infrastructure — both go through DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping. The difference is what comes out. Traditional Spring MVC with @Controller returns HTML pages rendered by a template engine like Thymeleaf — the server builds the full HTML and sends it to the browser. Spring REST with @RestController returns data in JSON format — no view templates involved. Modern applications almost always use the REST approach with a separate frontend in React or Angular that calls the API. But you can mix both in a single Spring Boot application — some routes return HTML pages, other routes under /api return JSON.
